Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
Jeremiah was an eighteen-year-old tax consultant who had been working at a small accounting firm in downtown Atlanta for just under a year when he finally scheduled an intake appointment. He arrived early, sat in the corner of the waiting room with his back to the wall, and did not remove his coat. When the therapist opened the door, he flinched—a small, sharp movement he tried to cover by reaching for his phone. He apologised before he sat down.

The event that had reshaped his life had happened two years earlier, during his junior year of high school in a suburb of Chicago. A classmate—someone he had considered a friend—had invited him to an empty apartment after school, claiming they needed help studying. Jeremiah remembered the door slamming shut behind him, the sound of the deadbolt turning. He remembered the shouting. The other boy had screamed at him, pinned him down, and raped him. Jeremiah had tried to push him off, but he was smaller, and the shouting had frozen something inside him. Afterward, he had walked home in a daze, tasting blood in his mouth—a metallic, coppery taste that he could still summon without warning, even now, in a therapist’s office. The taste would appear in the middle of a conversation, and he would feel the full weight of that afternoon crash over him, even when no image came with it. Other times, the memories were purely visual: snapshots of the ceiling, the pattern on the linoleum floor, the angle of the other boy’s jaw as he yelled.

For months afterward, Jeremiah had told no one. He graduated, moved to Atlanta for a job a family friend had arranged, and told himself the past was behind him. But the city was unfamiliar, and unfamiliar places felt dangerous in a way he could not explain. He could not assess the risk of a new coffee shop or a different bus route, so he stuck to the same two-block radius: his apartment, his office, the bodega on the corner. At work, he was a good tax consultant—methodical, quiet, reliable—but he had refused every invitation to after-hours drinks or team lunches. His coworkers assumed he was antisocial. What they did not know was that being alone with any man, even a colleague he had known for months, made his throat close up. He had developed a system: he always sat nearest the door in meetings, he never rode the elevator with only one other person, and he left the office the moment the last female coworker walked out.

The triggers that governed his days were specific and unrelenting. A door opening or slamming anywhere in the office building sent a spike of adrenaline through him; he would freeze, mid-keystroke, until he located the source of the sound. Shouting—even a raised voice in a nearby cubicle, even laughter that was too loud—made his hands shake. And strangers approaching him on the street, even to ask for directions, felt like an ambush. He had developed a habit of crossing the street whenever he saw a man walking toward him, and he had memorised every alternate route between his apartment and his office so that he never had to walk through a narrow alley or a quiet corridor.

The worst moments, though, were the ones that came without warning. He would be sitting at his desk, reviewing a client’s deductions, and suddenly his mouth would fill with the taste of that afternoon—copper, salt, something metallic—and his heart would hammer and his vision would narrow, and he would have no image in his mind, only the pure, raw feeling of terror. He had learned to press his fingernails into his palm until the pain grounded him, but he had also started drinking after work, just enough to dull the edge of those intrusions.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment that broke through all his careful systems. A male client had come in for a consultation, and Jeremiah had been assigned to meet with him alone in a small conference room. The client had leaned across the table to point at a line on a spreadsheet, and his hand had brushed Jeremiah’s wrist. The touch was light, accidental, and entirely ordinary—but Jeremiah had jerked back so violently that his chair tipped over, and he had ended up on the floor, gasping, while the client stared at him in confusion. His supervisor had pulled him aside afterward and asked, gently, if everything was all right. Jeremiah had said yes, but he knew he was not all right. He was afraid of what would happen if the next touch came in a context he could not escape. He was afraid his body would betray him again. And beneath that, what he hoped for—what he could barely admit to himself—was that someone might help him understand why a taste, a sound, a door closing, could still have so much power over him, two years and a thousand miles away from the room where it happened.
